People Who Never Reached Age 68

Leonardo da Vinci

Birth date: April 14, 1452

Death date: May 1, 1519

Age: 67

Leonardo da Vinci was the Italian Renaissance polymath whose paintings, anatomical studies, engineering designs, and notebooks made him one of history’s most influential artists and thinkers. Best known for the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, he spent his final years in France under royal patronage. He died at Clos Lucé near Amboise on 2 May 1519, aged 67, possibly after a stroke.

George Washington

Birth date: February 21, 1732

Death date: December 13, 1799

Age: 67

George Washington was a Virginia planter, military commander, Founding Father, and the first president of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797. He led the Continental Army to victory in the American Revolutionary War and helped establish many precedents for the presidency. He died at Mount Vernon on December 14, 1799, after a sudden severe throat illness, with later medical discussion often pointing to epiglottitis and the effects of aggressive bloodletting.

Adam Smith

Birth date: June 15, 1723

Death date: July 16, 1790

Age: 67

Adam Smith was a Scottish moral philosopher and political economist whose The Theory of Moral Sentiments and The Wealth of Nations helped shape modern economics, classical liberalism, and debates about markets, labor, and prosperity. He died in Edinburgh on 17 July 1790 after a painful illness, was buried in Canongate Kirkyard, and left instructions for unsuitable unpublished papers to be destroyed.

Karl Marx

Birth date: May 4, 1818

Death date: March 13, 1883

Age: 64
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Karl Marx is highly polarizing because his writings shaped revolutionary socialist and communist movements worldwide. Many readers associate Marxism with later one-party states, political repression, forced collectivization, and mass violence, even though Marx himself was a 19th-century theorist rather than a ruler.

Karl Marx was a German philosopher, economist, journalist, and revolutionary socialist whose analysis of capitalism and class conflict became one of the most influential bodies of political thought in modern history. With Friedrich Engels, he co-authored The Communist Manifesto, and his Das Kapital shaped later socialist, communist, and critical economic traditions. In his final years in London, Marx suffered declining health after the death of his wife Jenny; bronchitis and pleurisy followed a long period of illness, and he died there on 14 March 1883 at the age of 64.

Aristotle

Birth date: December 31, 384 BCE

Death date: December 31, 322 BCE

Age: 62

Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath from Stagira, a student of Plato and later tutor to Alexander the Great. His work shaped logic, biology, ethics, politics, metaphysics, rhetoric, and literary theory, and his Lyceum became the center of the Peripatetic school. After anti-Macedonian sentiment rose in Athens following Alexander’s death, Aristotle withdrew to Chalcis on Euboea, where he died in 322 BCE, traditionally associated with a longstanding stomach illness, at about 62.

Adolf Hitler

Birth date: April 19, 1889

Death date: April 29, 1945

Age: 56
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Extremely controversial because he was the Nazi dictator whose regime initiated the Second World War in Europe and carried out the Holocaust and other mass murders, persecutions, and aggressive wars.

Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician, leader of the Nazi Party, and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. His regime launched the Second World War in Europe and was central to the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims. In April 1945, with Berlin surrounded by Soviet forces and Nazi Germany collapsing, Hitler withdrew into the Führerbunker and died by suicide on 30 April 1945, aged 56.

William Shakespeare

Birth date: April 22, 1564

Death date: April 22, 1616

Age: 52

William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet, and actor from Stratford-upon-Avon, celebrated as the leading dramatist of the English language. His plays, sonnets, and narrative poems shaped world literature and theatre for centuries. He died in Stratford on 23 April 1616, traditionally his 52nd birthday; the precise cause of death is not known, though he was buried two days later at Holy Trinity Church.

Muhammad

Birth date: April 21, 570

Death date: June 7, 632

Age: 62
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Muhammad is a deeply revered religious figure for Muslims and also a historically contested political and military leader. Discussion of his wars, marriages, succession, lawgiving, and any visual depiction of him can be highly sensitive, and his legacy is often drawn into modern religious and political conflict.

Muhammad was an Arab religious, political, and military leader from Mecca who founded Islam and proclaimed the revelations that became the Qur'an. He united much of Arabia through preaching, diplomacy, and conflict, and his teachings became central to one of the world's major religions. In 632, shortly after the Farewell Pilgrimage, he fell ill in Medina with fever and severe pain and died in the house of his wife Aisha, leaving a rapidly expanding Muslim community without a clearly uncontested succession.

Michael Jackson

Birth date: August 28, 1958

Death date: June 24, 2009

Age: 50
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Michael Jackson is highly controversial because of repeated allegations of child sexual abuse, major criminal and civil proceedings, and later documentary accounts that kept public debate active after his death. He was acquitted in his 2005 criminal trial and denied the allegations, so the controversy includes both serious accusations and disputed legal/public interpretations.

Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, dancer, and global pop icon whose music, videos, choreography, and style reshaped popular entertainment. From his childhood with the Jackson 5 to solo milestones such as Off the Wall, Thriller, Bad, and Dangerous, he became one of the best-selling and most influential performers in history. He died in Los Angeles on June 25, 2009, at age 50, from cardiac arrest linked to acute propofol and sedative intoxication while preparing for his This Is It concert series.

Johann Sebastian Bach

Birth date: March 30, 1685

Death date: July 27, 1750

Age: 65

Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer, organist, and master of the late Baroque era, celebrated for works such as the Brandenburg Concertos, the St Matthew Passion, The Well-Tempered Clavier, and the Mass in B minor. His music combined intellectual architecture, expressive depth, and spiritual intensity in a way that shaped Western classical music for centuries. In his final years he suffered from severe eye problems; after unsuccessful eye surgery and a reported stroke, he died in Leipzig on 28 July 1750 at the age of 65.

Birth date: November 6, 1867

Death date: July 3, 1934

Age: 66

Marie Curie, born Maria Skłodowska, was a Polish-born French physicist and chemist whose pioneering work on radioactivity led to the discovery of polonium and radium and made her the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two scientific fields. She died in 1934 at age 66 from aplastic anemia, widely linked to years of radiation exposure during her laboratory research and World War I X-ray work.

Vladimir Lenin

Birth date: April 21, 1870

Death date: January 20, 1924

Age: 53
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Lenin is highly controversial because he founded and led a one-party revolutionary state, used political repression against opponents, and is associated with the Red Terror, civil-war coercion, censorship, and the creation of institutions that shaped later Soviet authoritarianism.

Vladimir Lenin, born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, was a Russian revolutionary, Marxist theorist, founder of the Bolshevik faction, and the first head of government of Soviet Russia and later the Soviet Union. He led the October Revolution of 1917 and shaped the one-party Soviet state through policies including nationalization, civil-war centralization, and the New Economic Policy. After a series of debilitating strokes in 1922 and 1923, Lenin’s health collapsed; he died at Gorki on 21 January 1924 at the age of 53.

Martin Luther was a German priest, theologian, professor, author, and former Augustinian friar whose Ninety-five Theses helped ignite the Protestant Reformation. His ideas on faith, scripture, and church authority reshaped Christianity and European history. He died in Eisleben, the town where he had been born, after years of declining health and during a visit connected with settling a local dispute.

Age: 55
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Julius Caesar is controversial as a conqueror and authoritarian political leader. His campaigns in Gaul caused mass death, enslavement, and displacement, and his crossing of the Rubicon, civil war, and dictatorship helped destroy the Roman Republic.

Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author whose conquest of Gaul, alliance with Pompey and Crassus, victory in civil war and dictatorship reshaped the Roman Republic and helped prepare the Roman Empire. After accepting the title dictator for life in 44 BC, he was stabbed to death by a senatorial conspiracy led by Brutus and Cassius on the Ides of March, an assassination that triggered another round of civil wars.

Ludwig van Beethoven

Birth date: December 15, 1770

Death date: March 25, 1827

Age: 56

Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist whose music helped drive the transition from the Classical era to Romanticism. Born in Bonn and later based in Vienna, he transformed the symphony, sonata, concerto, and string quartet, creating works such as the Fifth and Ninth Symphonies, Fidelio, the late piano sonatas, and the late quartets. His growing deafness made his career even more extraordinary. After several months of serious illness marked by symptoms such as jaundice, swelling, and abdominal fluid, he died in Vienna on 26 March 1827 at the age of 56.

Birth date: January 29, 1882

Death date: April 11, 1945

Age: 63

Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often known as FDR, was the 32nd president of the United States and the only American president elected four times. He led the country through the Great Depression with the New Deal and guided it through most of World War II, reshaping the role of the federal government. His health declined sharply during the war; while resting at Warm Springs, Georgia, he suffered a massive cerebral hemorrhage and died on April 12, 1945, shortly before victory in Europe.

Death date: September 13, 1321

Age: 56

Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet, political exile, philosopher, and author of the Divine Comedy, one of the defining works of world literature and a cornerstone of the Italian language. Banished from Florence in 1302, he spent his later life moving between Italian courts and completed his masterpiece in exile. He died in Ravenna in September 1321, aged 56, most likely from malaria contracted after returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau

Birth date: June 27, 1712

Death date: July 1, 1778

Age: 66

Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a Genevan philosopher, writer, composer, and one of the most influential voices of the Enlightenment. His ideas on popular sovereignty, education, inequality, emotion, and civic freedom shaped modern political thought and helped inspire later revolutionary movements in Europe. Best known for works such as The Social Contract, Émile, and Confessions, he blended philosophy with a strikingly personal literary style. Rousseau died suddenly at Ermenonville, France, on 2 July 1778, only four days after his 66th birthday; his death is generally attributed to cerebral bleeding or an apoplectic stroke.

Napoleon

Birth date: August 14, 1769

Death date: May 4, 1821

Age: 51
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Napoleon is highly controversial because his rule combined major legal and administrative reforms with authoritarian government, censorship, dynastic ambition, and years of large-scale war across Europe. His 1802 restoration of slavery in French colonies and the violent campaigns of the Napoleonic era are central reasons his legacy is disputed.

Napoleon Bonaparte, later Napoleon I, was a Corsican-born French general and statesman who rose during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French. He reshaped Europe through military campaigns, state reforms, and the Napoleonic Code, leaving a legacy admired for administrative modernization and criticized for war, authoritarian rule, and the restoration of slavery in French colonies. After his defeat at Waterloo, he was exiled to Saint Helena, where his health declined. He died at Longwood House on 5 May 1821, aged 51, most commonly attributed to stomach cancer.

Death date: February 8, 1881

Fyodor Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, journalist and thinker whose psychological fiction reshaped world literature. His major works include Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov, novels famous for their moral intensity, spiritual conflict and unforgettable characters. In his final days in Saint Petersburg, he suffered repeated pulmonary hemorrhages; after a last decline at home, he died on 9 February 1881 at the age of 59.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk

Birth date: May 18, 1881

Death date: November 9, 1938

Age: 57

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was the Ottoman-born soldier, statesman, and reformer who founded the Republic of Turkey and served as its first president from 1923 to 1938. A commander at Gallipoli and leader of the Turkish War of Independence, he reshaped the new republic through secular, legal, educational, linguistic, and cultural reforms. In his final year his health declined from liver disease, commonly identified as cirrhosis; he died at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul on 10 November 1938, aged 57.

Charles Dickens

Birth date: February 6, 1812

Death date: June 8, 1870

Age: 58

Charles Dickens was one of the defining writers of Victorian Britain, famous for novels such as Oliver Twist, David Copperfield, A Christmas Carol, Bleak House, A Tale of Two Cities, and Great Expectations. A former journalist and tireless public reader, he turned social injustice, poverty, childhood hardship, and urban life into unforgettable fiction. In his final years, heavy work and public readings strained his health; after suffering a final stroke at Gad's Hill Place in Kent, he died the next day on 9 June 1870, aged 58, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.

Age: 55

Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was a German philosopher, classical philologist, poet, and cultural critic whose work reshaped modern thought through ideas such as perspectivism, the critique of morality, the death of God, eternal recurrence, and the Übermensch. A former professor at Basel, he became an independent writer after years of illness. In 1889 he suffered a severe mental collapse and spent his final years incapacitated under family care. After strokes and pneumonia in 1900, he died in Weimar at the age of 55.

Walt Disney

Death date: December 14, 1966

Age: 65

Walt Disney was an American animator, film producer, voice actor, entrepreneur, and one of the defining figures of modern popular entertainment. He helped transform animation through Mickey Mouse, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, Disneyland, and a studio culture built around technical innovation and family storytelling. In late 1966, after being diagnosed with lung cancer, his health declined rapidly. He died in Burbank, California, on December 15, 1966, from circulatory collapse caused by the cancer, only ten days after turning 65.

Birth date: June 6, 1162

Age: 65
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Genghis Khan is extremely controversial because his conquests involved large-scale massacres, destruction of cities, forced submission, enslavement, and terror warfare across much of Eurasia, causing immense loss of life even though his empire is also studied for statecraft and military organization.

Genghis Khan, born Temüjin, was the Mongol leader who united the steppe tribes and founded the Mongol Empire in 1206, creating one of history’s most formidable military powers. His campaigns reshaped Eurasia, reaching deep into China and Central Asia. He died in August 1227, aged about 65, during the final campaign against Western Xia; later accounts link his decline to illness, possibly after a fall from a horse, and his burial place remains unknown.

Birth date: March 30, 1596

Death date: February 10, 1650

Age: 53

René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist whose method of radical doubt and famous idea “I think, therefore I am” helped shape modern philosophy. He also linked algebra and geometry, giving his name to Cartesian coordinates. In 1649 he moved to Stockholm to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden; the cold climate, early-morning lessons, and illness are traditionally connected with the pneumonia that led to his death on 11 February 1650, at age 53.

Christopher Columbus

Birth date: October 30, 1451

Death date: May 19, 1506

Age: 54
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Christopher Columbus is highly controversial because his voyages are tied to European colonization of the Americas, Indigenous dispossession, forced labor, enslavement, violence, and catastrophic population loss. He is also criticized for his conduct as governor in the Caribbean and for becoming a symbol in modern debates over conquest and colonial memory.

Christopher Columbus was a Genoese navigator and explorer whose four Spanish-sponsored Atlantic voyages transformed European knowledge of the Americas and helped launch a long era of exploration, conquest, and colonization. Ambitious, skilled, and controversial, he sought a westward route to Asia but reached Caribbean lands instead. After years of illness, disputes over titles and revenues, and declining royal favor, he died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506, still convinced he had reached the fringes of Asia. He was 54.

Death date: June 20, 1527

Age: 58

Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, political thinker, historian, playwright, and author whose sharp analysis of power made The Prince one of the most influential political books ever written. He served the Florentine Republic during a turbulent Renaissance era of shifting alliances, Medici rule, and foreign invasion. After losing office, he wrote the works that made his name synonymous with hard-headed political realism. He died near Florence in 1527, aged 58, after suffering from a stomach illness; he received last rites and was later buried in the Basilica of Santa Croce.

Age: 63

Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, printmaker, and draughtsman, celebrated for his psychological depth, dramatic light, self-portraits, biblical scenes, and portraits such as The Night Watch. He achieved great success in Amsterdam but later faced bankruptcy, family losses, and changing artistic tastes. Rembrandt died in Amsterdam on 4 October 1669 at age 63, after outliving his partner Hendrickje Stoffels and his son Titus. He was buried shortly afterward in the Westerkerk, with no grand public memorial recorded.

Woodrow Wilson

Birth date: December 27, 1856

Death date: February 2, 1924

Age: 67
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Woodrow Wilson is highly controversial because of his racist views and policies, including segregation in parts of the federal government, tolerance of white supremacist cultural politics, and his administration's treatment of Black Americans. His presidency is also criticized for wartime restrictions on civil liberties, political repression during World War I, and interventionist foreign policy.

Woodrow Wilson was the 28th president of the United States, a former Princeton University president and governor of New Jersey, and a central figure in World War I diplomacy and the League of Nations. His legacy combines major Progressive Era reforms and the Nobel Peace Prize with serious criticism of his racial policies. After a severe stroke in 1919 left him weakened and partly disabled, his health declined after leaving office, and he died at his Washington, D.C. home on February 3, 1924, aged 67.

Known for his intense product vision, he helped bring the Macintosh, iPod, iPhone, and iPad into popular culture. Cicero

Birth date: January 2, 106 BCE

Death date: December 6, 43 BCE

Age: 63

Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer, philosopher, writer, and one of the greatest orators of the late Roman Republic. As consul in 63 BCE, he opposed Catiline’s conspiracy and later became a powerful defender of republican government through his speeches, letters, and political thought. After attacking Mark Antony in the Philippics, Cicero was proscribed during the power struggle of the Second Triumvirate. He was captured near Formiae and assassinated on Antony’s order at age 63.

Ernest Hemingway

Birth date: July 20, 1899

Death date: July 1, 1961

Age: 61

Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist whose spare, forceful prose reshaped 20th-century fiction. A central voice of the Lost Generation, he wrote classics such as The Sun Also Rises, A Farewell to Arms, For Whom the Bell Tolls, and The Old Man and the Sea, winning the Pulitzer Prize and the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. His public image mixed literary discipline with travel, war reporting, fishing, hunting, and danger. After years of injuries, declining health, depression, and treatment, Hemingway died by suicide at his home in Ketchum, Idaho, on July 2, 1961, aged 61.

In his final months at Aachen, he fell ill with fever, developed pleurisy, and died on 28 January 814 before reaching his next birthday.

Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician, journalist, and dictator who founded Fascism and ruled Italy as Il Duce from 1922 until his overthrow in 1943. He turned Italy into a one-party dictatorship, aligned with Nazi Germany, and led the country into World War II. Herodotus was a Greek historian and geographer from Halicarnassus, best known for the Histories, his wide-ranging account of the Greco-Persian Wars, imperial power, travel, customs, and storytelling across the ancient Mediterranean and Near East. Cicero later called him the “Father of History,” a title that reflects both his ambition and his lasting influence. He appears to have died around 425 BCE, probably in late middle age, with ancient tradition associating his final years with Thurii in southern Italy or, less certainly, Pella in Macedon. No reliable account preserves the cause of his death, so his age at death is best estimated as 59.

Indira Gandhi was one of the defining political figures of modern India: the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, a central leader of the Indian National Congress, and India’s first female prime minister. She governed from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 to 1984, shaping India through war, reform, centralization of power, and the controversial Emergency. On 31 October 1984, at age 66, she was assassinated in New Delhi by two of her Sikh bodyguards after tensions following Operation Blue Star.

John Maynard Keynes was an English economist, mathematician by training, public intellectual, and one of the most influential economic thinkers of the twentieth century. His work reshaped modern macroeconomics, especially through Keynesian economics and the argument that governments could use spending, taxation, and monetary policy to fight recessions and mass unemployment. During and after the Second World War he also played a major role in designing the postwar financial order. Exhausted by public service and international negotiations, he suffered a series of heart attacks in 1946 and died at his home near Firle, Sussex, aged 62.

After leaving office, Johnson returned to his Texas ranch; he died there after a final heart attack on January 22, 1973, at the age of 64.

In Mexico City, after surviving an earlier attack, he was fatally wounded by Ramón Mercader, an assassin linked to Soviet intelligence, and died the next day at age 60.

Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador, military commander, explorer, and later Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca. Born in Medellín, Castile, around 1485, he went to the Caribbean before leading the 1519 expedition that, through warfare, diplomacy, Indigenous alliances, and the siege of Tenochtitlan, helped bring down the Aztec Empire and place much of central Mexico under Castilian rule. In later life he struggled with debt, court disputes, and fading political influence. While attempting to press his claims and hoping to return to Mexico, he became ill near Seville and died at Castilleja de la Cuesta on 2 December 1547, probably from dysentery and pleurisy.

David Hume was a major Scottish Enlightenment philosopher, historian, economist, and essayist, best known for his empiricism, skepticism, and searching analyses of human nature, causation, religion, morals, and politics. His works, including A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, made him one of the most influential thinkers in English-language philosophy. In his final year he suffered from an incurable intestinal illness, often described as intestinal cancer. He prepared calmly for death, completed a short autobiography, and died at his Edinburgh home on 25 August 1776, aged 65.

Birth date: December 30, 1491

Death date: August 31, 1557

Age: 65

Jacques Cartier was a Breton-French navigator whose three voyages between 1534 and 1542 opened the Gulf of Saint Lawrence and the Saint Lawrence River to French exploration. He helped give Canada its name and laid groundwork for later French claims in North America, though his colonization attempt at Charlesbourg-Royal failed. After returning to Saint-Malo, he lived out his final years away from major expeditions. He died there on 1 September 1557, aged 65, during an epidemic often described as possibly typhus, though the precise cause remains uncertain.

Death date: April 5, 1528

Age: 56

Albrecht Dürer was the defining artist of the German Renaissance: a painter, engraver, printmaker, and theorist whose woodcuts, engravings, portraits, and studies of proportion carried his reputation across Europe. He worked from Nuremberg, travelled to Italy and the Low Countries, and became admired by artists and patrons far beyond Germany. After returning from the Netherlands in 1521, he suffered years of failing health and produced less art while focusing on theoretical writings. He died in Nuremberg on 6 April 1528, aged 56, and was buried in the Johannisfriedhof cemetery.

Matsuo Bashō was the great Edo-period Japanese poet who transformed haikai and later became celebrated as the supreme master of haiku. Born near Ueno in Iga Province, he built a life around teaching, travel, literary experiment, and sharply observed scenes of nature and impermanence. His travel writing, especially the journey associated with The Narrow Road to the Deep North, helped make wandering itself part of his artistic legend. In 1694, while traveling again, Bashō fell ill in Osaka, apparently from a stomach ailment, and died there on November 28 at about age 50, surrounded by the aura of the road that had shaped his poetry.

His final years were marked by severe tuberculosis; after completing Nineteen Eighty-Four, he was treated in hospital in London, where he died from the disease on 21 January 1950 at the age of 46.

Why this is controversial: Qin Shi Huang was an authoritarian imperial ruler whose legacy includes wars of conquest, harsh Legalist punishments, forced labor on enormous state projects, censorship, and traditional accounts of book burning and executions of scholars. Some details of those accounts are debated, but his rule is strongly associated with coercive centralized power.

Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, was the founder of the Qin dynasty and the first emperor of a unified China. After defeating the rival Warring States, he centralized rule, standardized writing, weights, measures and coinage, expanded roads and walls, and left behind the famous mausoleum guarded by the Terracotta Army. He died in 210 BC during his fifth inspection tour of eastern China after becoming seriously ill; later tradition links his final years to an obsession with immortality, and mercury-based elixirs have often been suggested as a possible factor, though the exact cause remains uncertain.

Death date: July 30, 1875

Age: 66
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Andrew Johnson is one of the most controversial U.S. presidents. He opposed many Reconstruction protections for formerly enslaved people, clashed with Congress over civil rights and readmission of former Confederate states, used openly racist rhetoric, and became the first U.S. president to be impeached.

Andrew Johnson was the 17th president of the United States, a Tennessee Democrat and former tailor who rose from poverty to national office. He became president after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination and led the country through the turbulent early years of Reconstruction, becoming the first U.S. president to be impeached. After returning to politics as a U.S. senator, he suffered strokes while visiting his daughter in Tennessee and died on July 31, 1875, at age 66.

Kwame Nkrumah was the central leader of Ghana’s independence movement, the first prime minister of independent Ghana and later its first president. A forceful Pan-Africanist and political theorist, he helped found the Organisation of African Unity and became one of the most recognizable anti-colonial figures of the 20th century. Overthrown in a 1966 coup while abroad, he lived his final years in exile in Guinea. He died in Bucharest, Romania, on 27 April 1972 while receiving treatment for prostate cancer, aged 62.

Ivan Sergeyevich Turgenev was a Russian novelist, poet, playwright, translator, and one of the major voices of 19th-century realism. His story cycle A Sportsman’s Sketches helped shape Russian literary realism, while Fathers and Sons gave the world one of literature’s defining portraits of generational conflict and nihilism. In his final years he lived mostly in France, suffering from a painful malignant tumor that spread to his spine. He died at Bougival, near Paris, on 3 September 1883, aged 64, and was later buried in Saint Petersburg.

Marcel Proust was a French novelist, critic, and essayist whose monumental seven-volume work In Search of Lost Time transformed modern fiction through its exploration of memory, desire, art, society, and time. Long troubled by severe asthma and fragile health, he spent his final years increasingly confined while still revising his great novel. He died in Paris on 18 November 1922 from pneumonia and pulmonary complications at the age of 51.

Max Weber was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist whose work helped shape modern sociology and social theory. He is especially remembered for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, his analysis of bureaucracy, authority, rationalization, and the role of ideas in economic life. After the First World War, he advised on Germany’s new constitutional order and returned to teaching in Munich. He died there on 14 June 1920 at age 56, from pneumonia often linked to the influenza pandemic, leaving major work unfinished.

In his final years his health was weakened by drinking and repeated horse-riding injuries. He died of a heart attack in Byhalia, Mississippi, on July 6, 1962, at the age of 64.

After leaving office, he returned to Northampton, Massachusetts, wrote and spoke publicly, and lived a comparatively quiet retirement. He died suddenly at home on January 5, 1933, from coronary thrombosis, a form of heart-related clotting, at the age of 60.

Peter the Great, born Peter I Alekseyevich Romanov, was Tsar of Russia and later the first Emperor of Russia. He is remembered for transforming Russia into a major European power through military reform, naval expansion, administrative restructuring, Westernizing cultural policies, and the founding of Saint Petersburg. His reign reshaped the Russian state and left institutions that endured long after him. In his final years he suffered serious urinary and bladder illness; he died in Saint Petersburg on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52, with later accounts describing complications including uremia and gangrene of the bladder.

Osama bin Laden was a Saudi-born militant leader and the founder of al-Qaeda, the extremist organization behind major terrorist attacks including the September 11 attacks in the United States. Born into a wealthy Saudi family, he became involved in jihadist networks during the Soviet-Afghan War and later built al-Qaeda into an international terrorist movement. He died at age 54 on 2 May 2011, when U.S. Navy SEALs killed him during a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan.

Jane Austen was an English novelist whose sharply observant fiction transformed the novel of manners and helped shape literary realism. Best known for Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Mansfield Park, Persuasion, and Northanger Abbey, she wrote with wit, irony, and unusual insight into class, marriage, money, and women’s limited choices in Georgian society. Her fame grew greatly after her death, and her books have remained central to English literature. In her final year she suffered a serious, poorly understood illness, moved to Winchester to seek medical help, and died there on 18 July 1817 at the age of 41; later theories have included Addison’s disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, lupus, tuberculosis, and cancer.

Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist whose rare command of both theory and experiment helped shape modern nuclear and particle physics. He died in Chicago on 28 November 1954 from stomach cancer, aged 53, after an illness that cut short one of the most influential scientific careers of the twentieth century.

Sun Yat-sen

Birth date: November 11, 1866

Death date: March 11, 1925

Age: 58

Sun Yat-sen, also known as Sun Zhongshan and Sun Wen, was a Chinese revolutionary, physician, and political leader whose work helped bring down the Qing dynasty and establish the Republic of China. He became the republic’s first provisional president in 1912 and later led the Kuomintang, earning a lasting reputation as a founding figure of modern China. In his final months he was gravely ill in Beijing; doctors found advanced cancer involving the liver, and later reassessments have pointed to gallbladder cancer that had spread. He died in Beijing on 12 March 1925 at the age of 58.

Hector Berlioz

Birth date: December 10, 1803

Death date: March 7, 1869

Age: 65

Hector Berlioz was a French Romantic composer, conductor, and critic whose bold orchestral imagination reshaped 19th-century music. He is best known for Symphonie fantastique, Harold in Italy, the Requiem, Roméo et Juliette, La Damnation de Faust, and the opera Les Troyens. A brilliant writer on instrumentation and a forceful critic, he won more recognition abroad than in much of Paris during his lifetime. His final years were shadowed by chronic illness, depression, the deaths of loved ones, and a serious fall after a trip to Nice; he weakened gradually and died at his Paris home on 1869-03-08, aged 65.

Frédéric Chopin

Birth date: February 29, 1810

Death date: October 16, 1849

Age: 39

Frédéric Chopin was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic era, celebrated for transforming piano music through his nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises, études, preludes, and ballades. Born near Warsaw and later based in Paris, he became one of music’s earliest international celebrities while writing with a deeply personal, poetic style. Long troubled by poor health, he died in Paris on 17 October 1849 at the age of 39, most commonly attributed to tuberculosis, with later medical discussion suggesting complications involving tuberculous pericarditis.

Death date: December 31, 481 BCE

Heraclitus of Ephesus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher active around 500 BCE, famous for the Logos, the unity of opposites, and the vision of reality as constant change. Later ancient biography says he withdrew from society, suffered from dropsy, and died at about 60 after a failed self-treatment.

Friedrich Schiller

Birth date: November 9, 1759

Death date: May 8, 1805

Age: 45

Friedrich Schiller was a major German playwright, poet, philosopher, and historian, central to Weimar Classicism and remembered for works such as The Robbers, Don Carlos, William Tell, and Ode to Joy. A close collaborator and friend of Goethe, he helped shape modern German literature and dramatic thought. Schiller’s final years were marked by serious chronic illness, especially lung disease often described as tuberculosis. He died in Weimar on 9 May 1805 at the age of 45, while still creatively active.

Joseph Conrad

Birth date: December 2, 1857

Death date: August 2, 1924

Age: 66

Joseph Conrad, born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski, was a Polish-born British novelist and short-story writer whose seafaring life and mastery of English prose shaped classics such as Heart of Darkness, Lord Jim, Nostromo, and The Secret Agent. Celebrated for moral tension, psychological depth, and dark imperial settings, he became one of the major figures of modern fiction. He died aged 66 on 3 August 1924 at his home, Oswalds, in Bishopsbourne, Kent, probably from a heart attack, leaving his final novel Suspense unfinished.

Mikhail Bakunin

Birth date: May 29, 1814

Death date: June 30, 1876

Age: 62
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mikhail Bakunin is controversial because he was a revolutionary anarchist who endorsed insurrectionary struggle and the destruction of state authority. His writings include intense anti-state and anti-religious rhetoric, and some of his texts and private writings contain antisemitic language and conspiracy-minded attacks on rivals.

Mikhail Alexandrovich Bakunin was a Russian revolutionary anarchist and political philosopher, one of the central figures of 19th-century anarchism and a fierce opponent of authoritarian socialism. He took part in European revolutionary movements, endured imprisonment and Siberian exile, escaped through Japan and America, and later shaped collectivist anarchist thought. In his final years his health deteriorated after a life of agitation, prison, and exile; he retired to Switzerland and died in Bern on 1 July 1876 at the age of 62.

Charles Baudelaire

Birth date: April 8, 1821

Death date: August 30, 1867

Age: 46

Charles Baudelaire was a French poet, essayist, translator, and art critic whose Les Fleurs du mal helped reshape modern poetry with its urban intensity, musical language, and unsettling beauty. A major influence on Symbolism and literary modernism, he also translated Edgar Allan Poe and wrote sharply about art and modern life. His final years were marked by debt, illness, and collapse: after a massive stroke in 1866, he suffered paralysis and aphasia, spent time in care in Brussels and Paris, and died in Paris on 31 August 1867 at the age of 46.

Simón Bolívar

Birth date: July 23, 1783

Death date: December 16, 1830

Age: 47

Simón Bolívar was a Venezuelan military and political leader known as El Libertador for his central role in the independence of Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru, and Venezuela from Spanish rule. A visionary but often controversial statesman, he tried to unite parts of South America under Gran Colombia and became a lasting symbol of Latin American independence. In his final months, exhausted, politically isolated, and ill, he withdrew toward the Caribbean coast and died near Santa Marta on 17 December 1830, officially reported as tuberculosis, at the age of 47.

Saladin

Death date: March 3, 1193

Age: 55

Saladin, born Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, was the Kurdish founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and the first sultan of Egypt and Syria. A central figure of the Crusades, he united much of the Muslim Near East, defeated the Crusaders at Hattin, and recaptured Jerusalem in 1187. He died in Damascus in March 1193 after a fever, shortly after the end of the Third Crusade, and was remembered for both military skill and personal generosity.

Blaise Pascal

Birth date: June 18, 1623

Death date: August 18, 1662

Age: 39

Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer whose work shaped projective geometry, probability theory, fluid mechanics, and religious philosophy. A prodigy from childhood, he designed early calculating machines and later wrote the influential Lettres provinciales and Pensées. After years of fragile health, his illness worsened sharply in 1662; he suffered convulsions in Paris, received last rites, and died the next morning at age 39.

Alan Turing

Birth date: June 22, 1912

Death date: June 6, 1954

Age: 41

Alan Mathison Turing was an English mathematician, logician, cryptanalyst and pioneering computer scientist whose work shaped theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence and modern computing. During the Second World War he played a crucial role at Bletchley Park in breaking German ciphers, including Enigma-related naval traffic. After the war he designed early stored-program computer concepts and explored mathematical biology. In 1952 he was prosecuted for homosexual acts and underwent hormone treatment instead of imprisonment. He died in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 7 June 1954 from cyanide poisoning; the inquest ruled suicide, though later discussion has noted that accidental poisoning cannot be entirely excluded.

Walter Scott

Birth date: August 14, 1771

Death date: September 20, 1832

Age: 61

Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist, poet, historian, and lawyer whose Waverley novels helped establish the historical novel as a major literary form. Works such as Ivanhoe, Waverley, Marmion, and The Lady of the Lake made him one of the most widely read writers of the nineteenth century. After years of intense work, debt, and declining health, he suffered strokes, returned from a failed restorative journey abroad, and died at his home, Abbotsford, on 21 September 1832 at the age of 61.

Freddie Mercury

Death date: November 23, 1991

Age: 45

Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar, was the electrifying lead vocalist and pianist of Queen, celebrated for his four-octave voice, theatrical stagecraft, and classics such as “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Somebody to Love,” and “We Are the Champions.” He helped turn Queen into one of rock’s most iconic bands, with his 1985 Live Aid performance remaining legendary. Diagnosed with AIDS in the late 1980s, he kept working in the studio almost until the end. He publicly confirmed his illness only one day before dying at his Kensington home from AIDS-related bronchial pneumonia at age 45.

C. S. Lewis was a Belfast-born British writer, literary scholar, broadcaster, and Christian apologist, best known for The Chronicles of Narnia, The Screwtape Letters, Mere Christianity, and his academic work at Oxford and Cambridge. A close friend of J. R. R. Tolkien and a member of the Inklings, he combined imagination, theology, and literary criticism with rare public appeal. After a period of serious illness involving kidney disease, his health declined in 1963; he collapsed at his home in Oxford and died of kidney failure on 22 November 1963, aged 64.

George Eliot

Birth date: November 21, 1819

Death date: December 21, 1880

Age: 61

George Eliot, born Mary Ann Evans, was one of the defining novelists of Victorian England, admired for the realism, moral complexity, and psychological depth of works such as Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss, Silas Marner, Middlemarch, and Daniel Deronda. Writing under a male pen name helped her work be judged seriously in a literary culture dominated by men. After marrying John Walter Cross in 1880 and moving to Chelsea, London, she became ill with a throat infection, made worse by long-standing kidney disease, and died on 22 December 1880 at the age of 61.

Gabriela Mistral, born Lucila Godoy Alcayaga, was a Chilean poet, teacher, journalist, and diplomat whose lyric voice made her one of Latin America’s defining literary figures. Her final years were spent largely in New York, where poor health limited her travel; she died in Hempstead, Long Island, after pancreatic cancer, aged 67.

Yuri Gagarin

Birth date: March 8, 1934

Death date: March 26, 1968

Age: 34

Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to travel into outer space. On 12 April 1961, aboard Vostok 1, he completed one orbit of Earth in a 108-minute flight, becoming an international symbol of the Space Race and a Hero of the Soviet Union. His only spaceflight made him one of the most celebrated figures of the 20th century. He died on 27 March 1968, aged 34, when the MiG-15UTI training aircraft he was flying with instructor Vladimir Seryogin crashed near Kirzhach; the exact cause remained disputed for decades.

Robert Koch was a German physician and microbiologist whose work helped build modern bacteriology. He identified the bacteria responsible for anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera, developed influential laboratory methods, and received the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his tuberculosis research. In April 1910 he suffered a heart attack and never fully recovered; he died in Baden-Baden on 27 May 1910 at the age of 66.

Ingrid Bergman was a Swedish actress whose luminous, natural screen presence made her one of the defining stars of classic cinema. Internationally celebrated for films such as Casablanca, Gaslight, Notorious and Anastasia, she won three Academy Awards and remained active across film, theatre and television for five decades. She died in London on 29 August 1982, her 67th birthday, after a long battle with breast cancer that had spread in her final years.

Raphael, born Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino, was one of the defining artists of the High Renaissance, celebrated for the clarity, harmony, and grace of works such as The School of Athens, his Madonnas, and the Vatican Rooms. He died in Rome on April 6, 1520, at age 37, probably after a sudden fever or acute illness, while still at the height of his artistic powers.

Baruch Spinoza, also known by his Latin name Benedictus de Spinoza, was a Portuguese-Dutch philosopher whose radical rationalism helped shape modern biblical criticism, Enlightenment thought, democratic political theory, and debates about God, nature, freedom, and the mind. Excommunicated from Amsterdam’s Portuguese-Jewish community in 1656, he lived independently as a thinker and lens grinder while writing works such as the Theological-Political Treatise and Ethics. He died in The Hague on 21 February 1677 at age 44, probably from a lung illness often linked to tuberculosis and possibly aggravated by glass dust from lens grinding.

Birth date: February 27, 1533

Death date: September 12, 1592

Age: 59

Michel de Montaigne was a French Renaissance writer, philosopher, statesman, and humanist whose Essais helped create the modern literary essay. A former magistrate and mayor of Bordeaux, he wrote with unusual intimacy about judgment, friendship, education, fear, illness, and the limits of certainty. He died at the Château de Montaigne at 59, after long suffering from kidney stones and, according to traditional accounts, a severe throat infection or peritonsillar abscess that impaired his speech near the end.

Death date: January 8, 1873

Napoleon III, born Charles-Louis Napoléon Bonaparte, was the first President of France and later Emperor of the French, ruling during the Second Empire. Nephew of Napoleon I, he promoted modernization, infrastructure expansion, and French influence abroad, but his reign collapsed after defeat in the Franco-Prussian War. Deposed in 1870, he lived in exile in England, where worsening health and bladder-stone operations preceded his death at Chislehurst on 9 January 1873.

William McKinley

Death date: September 13, 1901

Age: 58

William McKinley was the 25th president of the United States, a Republican leader associated with protective tariffs, industrial growth, the Spanish–American War, and a major expansion of American influence overseas. A Civil War veteran who rose from enlisted soldier to brevet major, he also served in Congress and as governor of Ohio. His presidency ended after he was shot by anarchist Leon Czolgosz at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo on September 6, 1901; infection and gangrene set in, and he died eight days later at age 58.

Age: 63

Guglielmo Marconi was an Italian inventor, electrical engineer, entrepreneur, and Nobel Prize-winning pioneer of wireless telegraphy whose work helped make long-distance radio communication practical. He founded the Marconi Company, shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics, and became one of the best-known figures in the early history of radio. In his final years he suffered repeated heart attacks while still involved in advanced radio and microwave work. He died in Rome on 20 July 1937, aged 63, after a fatal heart attack and was honored with a state funeral.

Emily Dickinson was an American poet from Amherst, Massachusetts, whose compressed, startlingly original poems transformed modern literature despite her publishing very little while alive. Her work is known for slant rhyme, sharp imagery, unconventional punctuation, and intense attention to nature, faith, solitude, and mortality. In her final years she suffered repeated illness and increasing weakness; she died at home on May 15, 1886, with Bright’s disease listed as the cause, though later research has suggested severe hypertension may have contributed.

He died in Warsaw on 14 April 1917 at age 57, reportedly of heart failure, and was buried in the Jewish cemetery on Okopowa Street.

Why this is controversial: J. Robert Oppenheimer is highly controversial because of his leading role in the Manhattan Project and the creation of the first nuclear weapons. His later opposition to some nuclear arms policies, communist associations, and security clearance hearing also made him a central figure in debates over science, war, state secrecy, and moral responsibility.

J. Robert Oppenheimer was an American theoretical physicist best known as the scientific director of the Los Alamos Laboratory during the Manhattan Project, where he helped lead the development of the first nuclear weapons. Brilliant, cultured, and controversial, he later became a symbol of the moral burden carried by scientists in the atomic age. After years in public life and academia, he was diagnosed with throat cancer in the mid-1960s, likely connected to heavy smoking, and died in his sleep at his Princeton home on February 18, 1967.

Du Fu was one of the towering poets of Tang China, remembered with Li Bai as a defining voice of classical Chinese literature. His poems transformed personal hardship, war, exile, failed official ambitions, and compassion for ordinary people into art of extraordinary moral force, earning him later titles such as Poet-Historian and Poet-Sage. His final years were marked by illness, poverty, and wandering after the An Lushan Rebellion; in 770 he died in Hunan, probably on or near a riverboat, aged 58.

Gregor Johann Mendel was an Austrian Augustinian friar, teacher, botanist, meteorologist and mathematician whose pea-plant experiments in Brno laid the foundation for modern genetics. Why this is controversial: Mohamed Morsi is a highly controversial political figure. He was Egypt's first democratically elected president, but his administration was accused by opponents of authoritarian tendencies, sectarian politics, economic mismanagement, and concentrating power through a disputed constitutional declaration. His removal by the military and later death in custody are themselves deeply contested parts of Egypt's modern political history.

Mohamed Morsi was an Egyptian engineer, academic, and politician who became Egypt’s first democratically elected president after the 2011 revolution. Affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood and its Freedom and Justice Party, he served from 2012 until he was removed by the military in 2013 amid mass protests. He spent his final years in custody facing several trials, and on 17 June 2019 he collapsed during a court session in Cairo and died soon afterward, with official reports citing a sudden medical episode while critics pointed to prison conditions and medical neglect.

During World War II he flew reconnaissance missions for France. On 31 July 1944, aged 44, his aircraft disappeared over the Mediterranean during a mission near Corsica and Marseille; wreckage was later found, but the exact cause of the crash remains uncertain.

After a brilliant teaching career in Baghdad, a spiritual crisis led him to withdraw, travel, and write some of his most influential works. Near the end of his life he returned to teaching briefly, then settled again in Tus, where he died quietly in December 1111 after prayer and retirement from public life.

Based in Geneva, he shaped the Reformed tradition through his Institutes of the Christian Religion, biblical commentaries, and teachings on divine sovereignty and predestination. In his final years his health declined severely, including lung trouble and other chronic illnesses. He preached his last sermon in February 1564, said farewell to Geneva’s ministers in April, and died in Geneva on 27 May 1564 at the age of 54. He was buried in an unmarked grave to avoid turning his tomb into a shrine.

He died at 67 in Aberdeen, Scotland, after suffering a heart attack during a lecture tour.

George Harrison was an English musician, songwriter, film producer, and spiritual seeker who became internationally famous as the lead guitarist of the Beatles. The SI unit of electric current, the ampere, is named for him, and his interests also reached into chemistry, philosophy, and scientific classification. Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English poet, literary critic, philosopher, and theologian, best known as a founder of English Romanticism and as the author of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Kubla Khan, and Biographia Literaria. A brilliant but troubled figure, he shaped literary criticism and helped bring German idealist thought into English culture. He spent his final years in Highgate under the care of physician James Gillman, struggling with long-term illness and opium dependency. Coleridge died there on 25 July 1834, aged 61, from heart failure complicated by a lung disorder possibly connected with his opium use.

Johan August Strindberg was a Swedish playwright, novelist, poet, essayist, and painter, widely regarded as a transformative figure in modern Swedish literature and European drama. His works, including The Red Room, Miss Julie, The Father, A Dream Play, and The Ghost Sonata, helped shape naturalist, expressionist, and modernist theatre. A restless experimenter and fierce public polemicist, he drew heavily on personal experience, social conflict, and psychological tension. In his final years he lived in Stockholm, where illness increasingly overtook him. After suffering pneumonia in late 1911 and worsening stomach cancer, he died on 14 May 1912 at the age of 63.

Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist and travel writer whose restless imagination produced Treasure Island, Kidnapped, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, and A Child's Garden of Verses. Born in Edinburgh and often weakened by chronic respiratory illness, he turned poor health and travel into literary energy, eventually settling in Samoa, where he became known as Tusitala, the teller of tales. On 3 December 1894, at his home in Vailima, he suddenly collapsed after speaking with his wife and died within hours, probably from a stroke or brain haemorrhage. George Berkeley was an Anglo-Irish philosopher, Anglican bishop, and one of the major figures of early modern empiricism. He is best remembered for immaterialism or subjective idealism, the view that material objects exist only as perceived ideas, and for works such as A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge and Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous. He served as Bishop of Cloyne and also wrote on vision, mathematics, religion, and medicine. In 1752 he moved from Cloyne to Oxford to be near and supervise his son George’s education. He died there on 14 January 1753, reportedly while his wife was reading to him, and was buried at Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford.

Nikolai Gogol was a Ukrainian-born writer of the Russian Empire whose stories, plays, and novel Dead Souls reshaped Russian literature with satire, grotesque comedy, folklore, and psychological strangeness. In his final years he became increasingly religious, anxious, and physically weakened; after burning manuscripts, including material from the second part of Dead Souls, he refused food and died in Moscow at the age of 42.

Why this is controversial: Paul Gauguin is highly controversial because of his relationships with very young girls in French Polynesia, his abandonment of family responsibilities, and the colonial, exoticizing lens through which he depicted Tahitian people. Modern discussion of Gauguin often separates his artistic influence from serious criticism of his conduct and colonial context.

Paul Gauguin was a French Post-Impressionist painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramist, and writer whose bold color, simplified forms, and Synthetist style helped move modern art beyond Impressionism. After years as a sailor and stockbroker, he devoted himself to art and became especially associated with Brittany, Tahiti, and the Marquesas. He died suddenly in Atuona on Hiva Oa in 1903, weakened by illness and pain; some accounts mention heart failure, morphine use, or other health complications. He was 54.

Death date: August 8, 117

Age: 63

Trajan, born Marcus Ulpius Traianus, was Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117 and one of the most admired rulers of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty. A capable general and administrator, he expanded Roman power through campaigns in Dacia and the East, sponsored major public works, and was later remembered as optimus princeps, the “best ruler.” In his final year he became seriously ill while returning from eastern campaigns and died at Selinus in Cilicia, far from Rome, before his ashes were eventually associated with Trajan’s Column.

Death date: September 20, 1558

Age: 58
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Charles V is controversial because his rule was tied to imperial warfare, religious repression, dynastic domination, and the expansion of Spanish colonial power in the Americas. His reign overlapped with conquest, forced conversion, persecution of religious dissenters, and systems of extraction that caused severe harm to subject populations.

Charles V was the Habsburg ruler whose crowns linked Spain, the Low Countries, Austria, parts of Italy, and the Holy Roman Empire, creating one of the most formidable dynastic powers of the sixteenth century. As Charles I of Spain, he also ruled during the expansion of Spain’s American empire. Worn down by war, religious conflict, and chronic gout, he abdicated much of his power and retired to the Monastery of Yuste in Spain, where he became seriously ill, likely with malaria, and died in the early hours of 21 September 1558 at age 58.

Age: 59
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Oliver Cromwell is highly controversial because he helped overthrow and execute Charles I, ruled through military-backed authority, and led brutal campaigns in Ireland, especially at Drogheda and Wexford. His legacy is sharply divided between reformer, revolutionary, dictator, and perpetrator of severe wartime atrocities.

Oliver Cromwell was an English soldier, parliamentarian and statesman who rose from provincial gentry to become one of the central figures of the English Civil Wars. A gifted cavalry commander for Parliament, he helped defeat the royalists, supported the trial and execution of Charles I, and later ruled England, Scotland and Ireland as Lord Protector. His legacy remains fiercely debated, admired by some for religious and political reform and condemned by others for military rule and brutal campaigns, especially in Ireland. He died at Whitehall in 1658, aged 59, probably after a severe illness involving malarial fever, urinary or kidney trouble, and likely sepsis.

Nicholas II, born Nikolai Alexandrovich Romanov, was the last Emperor of Russia, ruling from 1894 until his abdication during the upheaval of 1917. His reign saw industrial growth but also deep political unrest, the Russo-Japanese War, the 1905 Revolution, and the strains of World War I. After abdicating, he and his family were held by revolutionary authorities and were executed by Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918, ending the Romanov dynasty’s rule.

Jean-Baptiste Racine was one of the defining playwrights of French classicism, admired for the concentrated power and psychological precision of tragedies such as Andromaque, Britannicus, Bérénice, Phèdre, Esther, and Athalie. Racine died in Paris on 21 April 1699 at the age of 59, reportedly from liver cancer; he had wished to be buried at Port-Royal, and his remains were later transferred to Saint-Étienne-du-Mont.

Joseph Goebbels was a German Nazi politician, philologist, and one of Adolf Hitler’s closest associates, best known as the Reich Minister of Propaganda from 1933 to 1945. He shaped Nazi control of newspapers, radio, film, and public messaging, using propaganda to promote antisemitism, war mobilization, and loyalty to Hitler. In the final days of the Second World War, he remained in Berlin, briefly became Chancellor of Germany after Hitler’s suicide, and died by suicide with his wife Magda on 1 May 1945 after their six children had been poisoned.

Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet and writer born in Prague, widely regarded as one of the most important German-language literary figures of the modern era. His major works include Duino Elegies, Sonnets to Orpheus, The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, and Letters to a Young Poet. Restless and cosmopolitan, he lived and worked across Europe before spending his final years in Switzerland. He had been seriously ill for some time, and his condition was eventually diagnosed as leukemia. Rilke died at the Valmont sanatorium near Lake Geneva on 29 December 1926, aged 51.

Henry David Thoreau was an American naturalist, essayist, poet, philosopher, abolitionist, and leading figure of Transcendentalism. He is best remembered for Walden, his classic meditation on simple living in nature, and Civil Disobedience, a powerful argument against unjust government authority. In his final years his health declined from long-running tuberculosis, worsened after a cold and bronchitis; he died at his mother’s home in Concord, Massachusetts, on May 6, 1862, at age 44.

Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish economist, diplomat, and the second Secretary-General of the United Nations, serving from 1953 until 1961. He helped define the modern role of the UN chief through preventive diplomacy, peacekeeping, and a strong belief in an independent international civil service. His work during crises in the Middle East and Congo made him one of the most respected diplomats of the twentieth century. He died at age 56 when his aircraft crashed near Ndola, Northern Rhodesia, while he was traveling to negotiate a ceasefire during the Congo Crisis; the exact circumstances of the crash have remained the subject of later inquiries.

Robert Hooke was an English polymath whose work helped define seventeenth-century science: he investigated elasticity, microscopy, astronomy, instruments, architecture, and surveying, and his Micrographia popularized the microscopic world while helping introduce the word “cell” into biology. He died in London at Gresham College in March 1703, aged 67, after years of worsening health; accounts describe serious decline late in life, including blindness and swollen legs.

Late in life, after the Persian defeat at Marathon and while preparing renewed campaigns amid revolt in Egypt, his health failed. He died in 486 BCE after an illness and was buried in his rock-cut tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam.

Claudius, born Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus, was the fourth Roman emperor and a member of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Long underestimated because of physical disabilities and his awkward public image, he unexpectedly came to power after Caligula’s assassination in AD 41. His reign strengthened imperial administration, expanded public works, and made Britain a Roman province. He died in Rome in AD 54 at the age of 63. Ancient writers commonly claimed he was poisoned, possibly with mushrooms, and suspicion has often fallen on his wife Agrippina, who benefited from Nero’s succession, though illness or natural causes remain debated.

In March 415, amid bitter civic and religious conflict, she was seized by a mob in Alexandria, dragged from her carriage, murdered, and her remains were destroyed, turning her death into one of antiquity’s most notorious attacks on learning and public reason.

Drake died on 28 January 1596 during a failed expedition near Portobelo, Panama, most likely from dysentery, and was buried at sea in a lead-lined coffin.

Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer whose observations helped establish that many so-called nebulae were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way and that the universe is expanding. His work reshaped observational cosmology and later gave his name to the Hubble Space Telescope. After a heart attack in 1949, he continued working on a reduced schedule; he died in San Marino, California, on 1953-09-28, most commonly reported from cerebral thrombosis. He was 63.

Maria Theresa was the powerful Habsburg ruler of Austria, Hungary, Bohemia and many other territories from 1740 to 1780, and the only woman to rule the Habsburg monarchy in her own right. She defended her inheritance during the War of the Austrian Succession and became known for major administrative, fiscal, military and educational reforms. In her final years she suffered worsening respiratory problems and edema; after falling seriously ill in November 1780, she died at the Hofburg in Vienna, with pneumonia and cardiopulmonary failure commonly cited in accounts of her last illness.

Amerigo Vespucci was a Florentine merchant, navigator and explorer whose accounts of Atlantic voyages helped Europeans understand that the lands west of the ocean were not Asia but a separate New World. His name inspired Martin Waldseemüller’s 1507 use of “America” on a world map. Vespucci spent his last years in Seville as Spain’s piloto mayor, responsible for navigation standards and charts. He died there on 22 February 1512, shortly before his 58th birthday, at age 57; some accounts connect his final decline with repeated bouts of malaria.

Pierre de Fermat was a French jurist, classical scholar, and one of the great mathematical minds of the seventeenth century. Working mostly outside academic institutions, he helped shape number theory, analytic geometry, probability, optics, and early ideas that later fed into calculus. His name is forever tied to Fermat’s Last Theorem, a marginal note that challenged mathematicians for centuries. He died in Castres on 12 January 1665, apparently after illness, and epitaph-based research indicates he was 57 years old.

At the start of the Spanish Civil War, he was arrested and executed by Nationalist forces near Granada; his body was never recovered, making his death one of the enduring tragedies of modern Spanish culture.

Empedocles of Acragas was a Greek pre-Socratic philosopher, poet, statesman, and religious thinker from Sicily. He is best known for teaching that the world is made from four roots—earth, water, air, and fire—moved by the opposing forces of Love and Strife. He also wrote in verse, argued against animal sacrifice, and developed ideas about reincarnation. His death was already legendary in antiquity: stories claimed he vanished, died abroad, or threw himself into Mount Etna, but the most defensible tradition says he died at about 60.

Why this is controversial: Ivan the Terrible is highly controversial because his reign included extreme autocratic violence, the oprichnina, mass repression, executions, confiscations, and the massacre of Novgorod. His expansion and state-building are inseparable from severe brutality.

Ivan IV Vasilyevich, known as Ivan the Terrible, was Grand Prince of Moscow and the first Tsar of Russia, ruling during a dramatic transformation of Muscovy into a more centralized and expansionist state. His reign included legal and military reforms, the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan, and the violent oprichnina that left a lasting mark on Russian history. He died in Moscow on 28 March 1584, traditionally said to have suffered a stroke while playing chess, leaving the throne to his son Feodor I.

After taking part in the Fronde and surviving serious wounds, he became a leading salon figure in Paris. He died in Paris at 66, after years of painful gout and declining health, remembered less for political success than for sentences that still sting with elegant precision.

In his final years he remained politically active despite illness and surveillance. He died in Pisa on 10 March 1872, reportedly from pleurisy, after returning secretly to Italy under the assumed name Brown; he was 66.

He founded the Ramakrishna Mission and helped shape modern Hindu thought and Indian nationalism. After years of intense travel, teaching, and declining health, he died quietly at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, reportedly while meditating; a cerebral blood vessel rupture has been suggested as a possible cause.

After later theological conflicts and failing health, he spent his final period under the protection of Peter the Venerable, died at the Priory of Saint-Marcel near Chalon-sur-Saône on 21 April 1142, and was eventually remembered alongside Héloïse as one of the great tragic figures of medieval Europe.

Robert E. Lee was a U.S. Army officer, West Point graduate, military engineer, and later the best-known Confederate commander of the American Civil War, leading the Army of Northern Virginia until its surrender in 1865. After the war he became president of Washington College in Lexington, Virginia. In his final years his health declined; he suffered a stroke in late September 1870 and died at his Lexington home on October 12, 1870, aged 63.

He is admired in some traditions and remembered painfully in others, especially in contexts shaped by Ottoman expansion.

Mehmed II, known as Mehmed the Conqueror, was the Ottoman sultan whose capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire and transformed the city into the empire’s great capital. A brilliant and ambitious ruler, he expanded Ottoman power across Anatolia and the Balkans while strengthening law, administration, architecture, and learning. In 1481, while setting out on another campaign, he became gravely ill near Gebze; gout was reported, and later accounts raised the possibility of poisoning. He died aged 49.

Moved between prison hospitals and clinics, he died in Rome on 27 April 1937 after a cerebral hemorrhage, aged 46.

Among his best-known poems are “Funeral Blues,” “September 1, 1939,” and “The Age of Anxiety,” the last of which helped secure his reputation as one of the major poets of the twentieth century. He died at 66 in Vienna, Austria, overnight after giving a poetry reading, with heart failure commonly cited as the cause; he was buried in Kirchstetten, Lower Austria.

Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer, Jacobin politician, and one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution. In July 1794, amid rising fear of his power and policies, he was overthrown in the Thermidorian Reaction, arrested, and guillotined in Paris without trial at the age of 36.

Ferdinand de Saussure was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher whose ideas reshaped the study of language in the 20th century. He published little in his lifetime; his most famous work, Course in General Linguistics, was reconstructed from students' lecture notes and published after his death. Saussure died from cancer on 22 February 1913 at Vufflens-le-Château, Switzerland, aged 55, leaving much of his influence to grow posthumously.

Nero was the fifth Roman emperor and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, reigning from AD 54 to 68. Remembered for his theatrical tastes, ambitious building projects, political violence, and the controversies surrounding the Great Fire of Rome, he remains one of antiquity’s most notorious rulers. Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

Death date: December 18, 1848

Age: 30

Emily Jane Brontë was an English novelist and poet, best remembered for her only novel, Wuthering Heights, a fierce and atmospheric classic of English literature published under the pen name Ellis Bell. Raised in the Yorkshire village of Haworth with her literary siblings Charlotte and Anne, she lived a largely private life shaped by the moors, family imagination, and intense creative discipline. Her health declined rapidly in 1848, soon after the death of her brother Branwell; she refused medical help until it was too late and died of tuberculosis in Haworth at the age of 30.

Gustav Klimt was an Austrian Symbolist painter and a founder of the Vienna Secession, celebrated for richly ornamental works such as The Kiss and Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I. In early 1918 he suffered a stroke and then developed pneumonia; he died in Vienna on 6 February 1918 at the age of 55.

Felix Mendelssohn was a German composer, pianist, organist, and conductor of the early Romantic era, admired for works such as A Midsummer Night’s Dream, the Italian and Scottish Symphonies, Elijah, the Violin Concerto, and Songs Without Words. Robert Burns was Scotland’s national poet, a brilliant lyricist in Scots and English whose works include "Auld Lang Syne", "Tam o’ Shanter", "To a Mouse", and "A Man’s a Man for A’ That". Born in Alloway to a farming family, he turned everyday rural life, love, satire, and radical sympathy for ordinary people into poetry with lasting international appeal. He spent his final years in Dumfries as an excise officer while continuing to collect and reshape Scottish songs. His health declined sharply in 1796; modern experts often link his death to endocarditis, probably connected with earlier rheumatic fever. He died in Dumfries on 21 July 1796, aged 37.

Park Chung Hee was a South Korean army officer and politician who ruled South Korea from his 1961 military coup through his presidency from 1963 to 1979. His government drove rapid industrialization and the so-called Miracle on the Han River, while also suppressing dissent under an authoritarian system. He was assassinated in Seoul on 26 October 1979 by Kim Jae-gyu, the head of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, during a private dinner near the Blue House.

Lev Davidovich Landau was a Soviet theoretical physicist whose work reshaped modern physics, especially condensed matter theory, superfluidity, quantum mechanics, plasma physics, and superconductivity. Awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physics for his theory of superfluidity in liquid helium, he was admired for his brilliance, range, and formidable scientific school. In 1962 he suffered catastrophic injuries in a car accident and spent weeks in a coma; although he survived, his creative scientific work never fully recovered. He died in Moscow on 1968-04-01 from complications linked to those injuries, at the age of 60.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Ancient sources portray him as cruel, arbitrary, sexually abusive, financially exploitative, and willing to use executions and humiliation to consolidate personal power. Modern historians debate how much of this reputation comes from hostile elite sources, but his public image remains strongly associated with tyranny and abuse.

Caligula, born Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from 37 to 41 CE; remembered for his volatile reputation, concentration of imperial power, and ambitious public works, he remains one of antiquity’s most debated rulers. In January 41 he was assassinated at the Palatine Games in a conspiracy led by Praetorian officers, ending his reign at age 28.

Babur, born Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad, was a Timurid prince, poet, memoirist, and military leader who founded the Mughal Empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. A descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, he combined Central Asian political ambition with literary talent, leaving the Baburnama as a major autobiographical work. He died in Agra on 26 December 1530, aged 47, and was succeeded by his son Humayun; his remains were later moved to Kabul in accordance with his wishes.

Extremely controversial historical figure

His populist image and charitable gestures are inseparable from a record of organized crime and terror.

Pablo Emilio Escobar Gaviria was a Colombian drug lord, narcoterrorist, politician, and founder of the Medellín Cartel, one of the most powerful cocaine-trafficking organizations of the late twentieth century. Known as the “King of Cocaine,” he combined extreme violence with populist gestures that made his legacy deeply controversial. After escaping from his self-built prison, La Catedral, he became the target of a major manhunt and was killed in Medellín on 2 December 1993 during a rooftop shootout with Colombian security forces, one day after turning 44.

Yukio Mishima, born Kimitake Hiraoka, was one of Japan’s most influential postwar writers, known for novels such as Confessions of a Mask and The Temple of the Golden Pavilion, as well as plays, essays, acting, and a highly stylized public persona. His work fused classical Japanese aesthetics with modern psychological intensity and recurring themes of beauty, discipline, nationalism, eroticism, and death. In 1970, after leading members of his private militia in a failed attempt to rouse Japan’s Self-Defense Forces, he died by seppuku in Tokyo at age 45.

Andrei Tarkovsky was a Soviet film director, screenwriter, and theorist whose meditative style, long takes, spiritual themes, and dreamlike imagery made him one of cinema’s most influential artists. Husayn ibn Ali was a central religious and political figure of early Islam: the son of Ali and Fatima, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, younger brother of Hasan ibn Ali, and revered in Shia Islam as the third Imam.
