Why this is controversial: Richard I of England is controversial because his reputation as a heroic crusader is inseparable from religious war, heavy taxation, dynastic conflict, and violence during the Third Crusade, including the mass execution of Muslim prisoners after the capture of Acre.

Richard I of England, remembered as Richard the Lionheart, was a Plantagenet king famed for his military skill, leadership in the Third Crusade, and rule over a wide Angevin realm that included England, Normandy, Aquitaine, and Anjou. Although he became an enduring symbol of chivalric kingship, he spent little of his reign in England. In 1199, while besieging Châlus-Chabrol in Aquitaine, he was struck by a crossbow bolt; the wound became gangrenous, and he died on 6 April at the age of 41.

Caravaggio, born Michelangelo Merisi, was an Italian painter whose intense realism, dramatic chiaroscuro, and tenebrism helped transform late Renaissance art into the Baroque style. Active mainly in Rome, Naples, Malta, and Sicily, he gave religious and mythological scenes a startling immediacy that influenced Rubens, Ribera, Velázquez, Rembrandt, and many others. His final years were turbulent after he killed Ranuccio Tomassoni and fled Rome. He died at 38 in Porto Ercole while trying to return toward Rome, traditionally reported as fever but still debated, with theories including infection, violence, or poisoning.

Frail for much of his life, he spent his last years in Naples with Antonio Ranieri. He died there suddenly at 38 during the 1837 cholera epidemic; the immediate cause is often described as pulmonary edema, heart failure, or dropsy, and Ranieri helped prevent his burial in a common epidemic grave.

He died on 3 July 1904 at age 44, after serious heart-related illness; some accounts also describe pneumonia and an exhausted, weakened heart after years of intense political work.

His work helped shape theories of comparative advantage, rent, wages, profits, and free trade, and his arguments against protectionism influenced later economic policy. He died on 11 September 1823 at Gatcombe Park, Gloucestershire, aged 51, after an ear infection reportedly spread and led to septicaemia.

Walter Benjamin was a German-Jewish philosopher, cultural critic, essayist, and media theorist whose writings on art, literature, history, technology, and modern urban life became central to twentieth-century critical theory. In 1940, while fleeing Nazi-occupied Europe through the French-Spanish border town of Portbou, he died by suicide after fearing deportation back to France and likely capture by the Nazis.

Srinivasa Ramanujan was an Indian mathematician whose extraordinary intuition transformed number theory, infinite series, continued fractions, partitions, and modular forms. Largely self-taught, he developed thousands of identities and formulas, many later proved correct and influential. His correspondence with G. H. In 1919, worsening illness forced him to return to India; he died in Kumbakonam on 26 April 1920, aged 32, while still producing new mathematical ideas.

He wrote works such as Mademoiselle de Maupin, Émaux et camées, and Le Capitaine Fracasse, and was admired by figures including Baudelaire, Flaubert, Proust, and Wilde. In his last years he lived through the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune in Paris; weakened by long-standing cardiac disease, he died at Neuilly-sur-Seine on 23 October 1872, aged 61, and was buried in Montmartre Cemetery.

In his final year he returned from Italy to Germany after securing the succession of his son Otto II. Alexander III of Russia was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1881 until 1894. A firm autocrat, he reversed many of Alexander II’s liberal reforms, promoted Russian nationalism, and became known as “the Peacemaker” because Russia fought no major wars during his reign. His later years were marked by declining health, and in 1894 he became gravely ill with kidney disease. Too weak to travel farther, he remained at Livadia in Crimea, where he died on 1 November 1894 at the age of 49.

Mary I, often called Mary Tudor, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1553 to 1558 and the first queen regnant of England. The daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, she tried to restore Roman Catholicism after the English Reformation and became notorious for the Marian persecutions of Protestants. Her marriage to Philip of Spain was politically divisive, and she left no child. She grew weak and ill in 1558, possibly from ovarian cysts or uterine cancer, and died at St James's Palace during an influenza epidemic at the age of 42.

Titus Flavius Vespasianus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 CE and a leading figure of the Flavian dynasty. Before ruling, he commanded Roman forces in the Jewish War and captured Jerusalem in 70, an event later commemorated by the Arch of Titus. As emperor he completed the Colosseum and became known for disaster relief after Vesuvius and a major fire in Rome. His reign was brief: after the amphitheatre games, he fell ill and died of fever on 13 September 81, aged 41, and was succeeded by his brother Domitian.

Shaka kaSenzangakhona, widely known as Shaka Zulu, was the powerful founder and king of the Zulu Kingdom, remembered for reshaping military organization, discipline, and regional politics in southern Africa. His reign from about 1816 to 1828 helped turn the Zulu from a smaller chiefdom into a major force. He was assassinated at KwaDukuza by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana, with Mbopa also traditionally named among the conspirators, after mounting tensions in the royal court.

John, King of England from 1199 to 1216, was the youngest son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine and is remembered as John Lackland. His reign saw the loss of Normandy to Philip II of France, conflict with the papacy, heavy taxation, and the baronial crisis that led to the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215. Selim I

Birth date: October 9, 1470

Death date: September 21, 1520

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Selim I is highly controversial because his reign involved aggressive imperial expansion, major wars against the Safavids and Mamluks, dynastic executions, and severe violence against groups seen as internal enemies, especially Qizilbash and Alevi-associated communities. His nickname, Selim the Grim, reflects a reputation for severity and brutality.

Selim I, known as Yavuz Sultan Selim or Selim the Grim, was the Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520. In only eight years he dramatically expanded Ottoman power, defeating the Safavids at Chaldiran and conquering the Mamluk Sultanate, bringing Syria, Egypt, the Hejaz, and key pilgrimage routes under Ottoman control. He died near Çorlu after a severe illness, traditionally linked to a badly treated carbuncle or boil, though later writers have suggested other causes such as cancer or plague.

E. T. A. Hoffmann

Birth date: January 23, 1776

Death date: June 24, 1822

Age: 46

E. T. A. Hoffmann was a German Romantic author, composer, jurist, music critic, and artist, remembered for darkly imaginative works such as The Sandman and The Nutcracker and the Mouse King, which later inspired Tchaikovsky’s ballet. His fiction helped shape fantasy, Gothic horror, and early crime writing. In his final months in Berlin he suffered a severe progressive paralysis, dictating late work when he could no longer write; he died on 25 June 1822, aged 46, probably from respiratory failure linked to that illness.

Death date: October 24, 337 BCE

Philip II of Macedon was the ambitious king who transformed Macedon from a peripheral kingdom into the dominant power of Greece. He rebuilt the army, perfected the Macedonian phalanx, used diplomacy and marriage alliances with ruthless skill, and prepared the campaign against Persia that his son Alexander the Great would later carry out. In October 336 BCE, while attending royal wedding celebrations at Aegae, Philip was stabbed by his bodyguard Pausanias of Orestis and died suddenly at about 46.

Simone Weil

Birth date: February 2, 1909

Death date: August 23, 1943

Age: 34

Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic, teacher, writer, and political activist whose short life left a lasting mark on political thought, religious philosophy, and ethics. Born in Paris to a secular Jewish family, she taught, supported labor movements, worked in factories to understand working-class life, and briefly joined anti-fascist forces during the Spanish Civil War. During World War II she worked with the Free French in Britain. Already weakened by illness, tuberculosis, and severe self-denial, she died in Ashford, Kent, from cardiac failure linked to poor health and restricted eating, aged 34.

Lesya Ukrainka, born Larysa Petrivna Kosach, was one of Ukraine’s great literary voices: a poet, playwright, translator, intellectual, and activist whose works such as Forest Song helped shape modern Ukrainian literature. She died in Surami, Georgia, after a long struggle with tuberculosis affecting her bones, lungs, and kidneys, with family caring for her in her final days.

Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and South Slav nationalist best known for assassinating Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, an act that helped set off World War I. Sentenced to prison because he was under 20, he died there in 1918 at age 23 from tuberculosis aggravated by harsh prison conditions.

Ryūnosuke Akutagawa was a Japanese writer of the Taishō period, celebrated for sharply crafted short stories such as Rashōmon, In a Grove, The Nose, and Hell Screen. Evangelista Torricelli was an Italian physicist and mathematician, remembered above all for inventing the mercury barometer and for work that helped clarify air pressure, motion, optics, and early ideas related to calculus. A pupil of Benedetto Castelli and later connected with Galileo’s circle in Florence, he became one of the sharpest scientific minds of seventeenth-century Italy. His career was brief: in October 1647 he died in Florence after a fever, most likely typhoid, only ten days after turning 39.

Germaine de Staël, born Anne Louise Germaine Necker, was a French-Swiss novelist, essayist, political thinker, and salonnière whose writing helped carry European thought from Enlightenment classicism toward Romanticism. After years of exile and restless travel, her health declined; she suffered a stroke in February 1817, was left partly paralyzed, and died in Paris on 14 July 1817 at the age of 51.

Julian, known as Julian the Apostate, was a Roman emperor, scholar, military commander, and philosopher who ruled from 361 to 363. Billie Holiday, born Eleanora Fagan and nicknamed “Lady Day,” was one of the most influential American jazz and swing singers of the twentieth century. Birth date: February 5, 1912

Age: 33
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Eva Braun is highly controversial because she was Adolf Hitler's longtime companion and briefly his wife, lived inside his private circle during the Nazi dictatorship, and is strongly associated with the leadership environment of a regime responsible for genocide, aggressive war, and mass persecution.

Eva Braun was a German photographer and the longtime companion of Adolf Hitler, whom she met while working for Heinrich Hoffmann, Hitler’s photographer. For years she lived largely out of public view, becoming part of Hitler’s private circle at the Berghof and leaving behind many photographs and films of that world. In the final days of Nazi Germany, she joined Hitler in the Berlin Führerbunker, married him on 29 April 1945, and died by suicide with cyanide the next day as Soviet troops closed in.

Birth date: January 3, 1809

Death date: January 5, 1852

Age: 43

Louis Braille was a French educator, musician, and inventor whose six-dot tactile writing system transformed literacy for blind and visually impaired people around the world. Blinded in childhood after an accident in his father’s workshop, he became a gifted student at the Royal Institute for Blind Youth and developed braille while still a teenager. He later taught at the Institute and refined his system for reading, writing, and music. Braille suffered for many years from a serious respiratory illness, widely described as tuberculosis, and died in Paris on 1852-01-06, just two days after turning 43.

Death date: November 1, 1930

Age: 50

Alfred Lothar Wegener was a German meteorologist, geophysicist, polar researcher, and the scientist who proposed the continental drift hypothesis, a once-ridiculed idea that later became central to plate tectonics. He also made important contributions to meteorology and Greenland exploration. During his 1930 Greenland expedition, he helped resupply the remote Eismitte station in extreme cold. After leaving with Rasmus Villumsen for the west coast, Wegener died on the ice, probably from exhaustion and heart failure; his body was found months later.

Jean-Paul Marat

Birth date: May 23, 1743

Death date: July 12, 1793

Age: 50
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Jean-Paul Marat is highly controversial because of his radical journalism during the French Revolution, his calls for harsh action against perceived enemies of the revolution, and his association with the political atmosphere that led to revolutionary violence and the Reign of Terror. His murder also turned him into a polarizing revolutionary martyr.

Jean-Paul Marat was a French revolutionary journalist, physician, scientist, and political theorist whose newspaper L'Ami du peuple made him one of the most uncompromising voices of the radical movement during the French Revolution. A fierce defender of the sans-culottes and a figure associated with the Montagnards, he became both influential and deeply divisive. Suffering from a severe skin condition, he often worked from a medicinal bath; on 13 July 1793, he was stabbed there by Charlotte Corday, a Girondin sympathizer, and soon became a revolutionary martyr.

Birth date: April 6, 1506

Death date: December 2, 1552

Francis Xavier was a Navarrese Catholic cleric, missionary, and co-founder of the Society of Jesus. A close companion of Ignatius of Loyola, he became one of the most influential Christian missionaries of the early modern era, working across India, Southeast Asia, and Japan and helping launch the first major Christian mission to Japan. In 1552 he tried to enter Ming China but was stranded on Shangchuan Island, where he fell ill while waiting for passage to the mainland. He died there on 3 December 1552 at the age of 46.

Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
